📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahmed Barakat is a journalist and copywriter based in Georgia with a growing focus on blockchain technology, DeFi, AI, privacy, digital assets, and fintech innovation.

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Crypto’s stablecoin market has shed $16 billion in a month, marking its sharpest contraction since the 2022 bear market. The retreat is hitting USDT and USDC hard, leaving fewer dollar-backed tokens circulating.

Industry observers note that total stablecoin market cap now stands at $283 billion, down more than 5% after losing $16.5 billion in a month. The decline puts the market under pressure just as crypto struggles to recover, with investors showing little appetite for buying the dip.

According to recent reports, tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC account for most of the latest contraction. USDT is holding a market cap of $175.02 billion, down 4.3% over 30 days, while USDC fell to $68.58 billion, losing 5% during the same period. Together, the two stablecoins represent 86% of the entire market.

The contraction also extends beyond dollar-backed tokens. Sky Dollar’s USDS supply dropped 22.32% over 30 days, while Ethena’s USDe expanded 4.36%. The gap shows that some are still moving between stablecoin products.

CryptoQuant data points the same way. CryptoQuant data published on November 11 showed USDT market cap had fallen $6.6 billion over 60 days through November 7. It was more than twice the $3.2 billion decline recorded after FTX collapsed in November 2022.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

The current contraction brings back an ugly history. Stablecoin supply reached $161.5 billion in March 2022 before entering a prolonged decline. Terra’s UST collapse accelerated the withdrawal of capital, with nearly $30 billion disappearing from stablecoin supply in June alone.

Sources indicate that that monthly decline was almost twice the latest $16.5 billion contraction. Back in 2022, the damage continued into the following year. By September 2023, aggregate stablecoin supply had fallen by 26% from its March 2022 peak, a contraction of $43 billion.

Bitcoin endured a similar period of weakness. After reaching nearly $69,000 in November 2021, BTC eventually plunged to around $15,500 in November 2022. Stablecoin supply continued shrinking even after the initial market shock initiated by Terra. Crypto’s liquidity problems then became a prolonged market condition.

Yet, in 2023, not every stablecoin experienced the same fate. USDT supply rose $13.3 billion from its November 2022 lows, while USDC lost $16.7 billion. During that period, investors were not simply abandoning every stablecoin. Some were moving toward Tether as the market reassessed issuers and available returns.

According to recent reports, this time, arguably, the stablecoin contraction is happening against a different market backdrop. Crypto traders have fewer reasons to keep large amounts of capital parked in stablecoins when Bitcoin and major altcoins struggle to attract buyers. Some holders may be redeeming their tokens for traditional dollars, while others are moving into interest-bearing assets outside crypto.

A shrinking stablecoin market does not mean every dollar has left digital assets. But the simultaneous decline in USDT and USDC supply makes the latest contraction harder to dismiss as simple rotation between issuers.

A crypto recovery needs buyers willing to commit fresh capital, and stablecoins have historically provided traders with an immediate way to enter the market.

  • People can instruct Gemini to launch a local app by including the command “@Computer use” in their prompts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:41 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Google LLC today released a fresh version of Gemini’s Mac client that can interact with other apps on the user’s computer.

Recent findings suggest that the feature is available in the U.S. on launch. It requires a Google AI subscription, which equips consumer Google accounts with a broader lineup of artificial intelligence tools. The offering also includes additional storage space and certain other features.

People can instruct Gemini to launch a local app by including the command “@Computer use” in their prompts. For example, a designer could upload a sketch of a vehicle and ask the AI assistant to turn it into a three-dimensional animation. Gemini finds the local app that is needed for the task, creates a project strategy and carries out the work step by step.

Industry observers note that the assistant supports tasks that comprise dozens of actions. Furthermore, consumers can use the output of a newly completed Gemini workflow to launch follow-up projects. A user could have the assistant generate a visual asset in a design tool and then turn it into a mini-app with Visual Studio Code.

It has been revealed that gemini can interact with not only local apps but also web services. That means it can load data from webpages into programs that run on the user’s machine, as well as move data in the opposite direction and between cloud services.

Industry observers note that the AI carries out its work in a background window. As a result, users don’t have to pause their work while the assistant is running. They can track Gemini workflows via a preview pane built into the Mac client’s chat window. Additionally, Google has included controls that make it possible to give Gemini feedback mid-task.

“Privacy and safety are built in: you choose which apps Gemini can access, watch every step live, pause at any time, and approve key actions before they happen,” Michael Friedman, Google’s group product manager for the Gemini app, wrote in a blog post.

Recent findings suggest that the Mac version of Muse, Meta Platforms Inc.’s recently debuted AI agent, can also interact with local apps and data. Furthermore, a cloud-based virtual machine enables it to perform tasks even when the user’s computer is offline. Dots, a competing service from OpenAI Group PBC, offers a similar capability.

Google may seek to match its rivals’ cloud-based workflow hosting features in the future. The organization can also extend Gemini in other ways. Notably, it could bring Gemini’s computer use mode to additional operating systems and add features for business customers. OpenAI’s Dots already includes capabilities designed to automate business workflows such as procurement.

SpaceX raised a record $75 billion in its IPO in June. The bottom for ETH came three trading days before SpaceX priced its shares, and the price of ETH went up after that.

It has been revealed that anthropic is set to price its IPO on Nov. 18 and aims to raise up to $64.4 billion. It would be the second-largest IPO in history after SpaceX.

Industry observers note that lee blamed the decline of ETH on a rotation of money into the Anthropic IPO, and Binance founder Changpeng Zhao and Strive CEO Matt Cole have pointed to the same flow of liquidity. On Monday, ETH is trading at $1,823.

In a recent development, bitMine Immersion Technologies (BMNR), which Lee chairs, has bought ETH every week since it launched its treasury strategy on June 30, 2025. In its Nov. 16 patch, the tech giant disclosed fresh numbers: it added 7,653 ETH to its reserves last week and 9,587 ETH the week before.

In a recent development, bitMine now holds 6,077,745 ETH, or 4.97% of all coins in circulation (about 122.2 million ETH), and it is the world's largest corporate Ethereum treasury. According to the company, it is 99% of the way through its "Alchemy of 5%" program, and fewer than 35,000 ETH are left to reach the target.

The total portfolio of BitMine, which includes crypto, cash, securities and venture stakes, has shrunk from a peak of more than $14 billion to $11.8 billion. According to BitMine, 5,227,037 ETH, or around 86% of the reserve, is staked.

Lee expects the growth cycle for ETH to last two to three years, driven by bank tokenization, and his base-case targets for ETH range from $12,000 to $22,000.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of substantial news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

According to recent reports, the Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

It has been revealed that finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are Fresh York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

It has been revealed that chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At first glance, Latest Hope, PA, looks like little more than a picturesque, upscale river town with a vibrant arts scene. However, a closer look reveals that the historic borough shares an architectural DNA with Europe's premier capitals.

Located halfway between Fresh York City and Philadelphia, New Hope spans roughly 1.42 square miles and is home to fewer than 3,000 year-round residents. Yet it boasts an outsized reputation as a beloved regional tourist destination renowned for its art galleries, boutiques, riverside dining, and cultural institutions, led by the iconic Bucks County Playhouse, which has hosted major stars such as Grace Kelly, Robert Redford, and Liza Minnelli.

In Latest Hope's luxury housing market, old and new blend seamlessly: 18th-century structures are brought into the 21st century with bold, modern additions and amenities.

"A lot of the homes around here, especially some of the larger homes, all started off as an old stone farmhouse, so incorporating some of that character while building the big steel and glass additions is very much an architectural vibe that is done here," Nicholas Esser, managing partner at Addison Wolfe Real Estate, tells Realtor.com®.

The market's remarkably varied housing stock also includes stately Colonial and Victorian homes, sprawling legacy estates, and cutting-edge latest construction that would not look out of place in the heart of Silicon Valley.

Recent findings suggest that architect Ralph Fey, with Ralph C. Fey Architects in Doylestown, PA, explains that Fresh Hope's signature look is rooted in regulatory necessity, because more than half of the town falls in a strictly regulated historic district, which rarely allows older buildings to be torn down to make way for new builds.

Rather than viewing zoning laws as a creative roadblock, Fey has made his professional mark by seamlessly merging history with contemporary living.

Sources indicate that "Some of the best architecture is born out of constraints," he tells Realtor.com. "The goal, the fun, the challenge is how to maintain that historic feel, meet the guidelines of the historic district, but provide the amenities that we now want to have as we live on the water.".

Recent findings suggest that maureen Reynolds, a Serhant luxury real estate agent in Latest Hope, counts herself among Fey's clients. She right now lives in an 1832-built converted horse barn with tall ceilings and hand-hewn beams.

"I have all the modern amenities because of Ralph," she tells Realtor.com.

While New Hope lacks the urban density and wealth of major metros, Fey says, its architectural style "is more like London, where you have newer construction next to historic construction, next to really historic construction, and it is that fabric that makes London so exciting.".

Founded in the 18th century on the banks of the Delaware River, Newly introduced Hope was previously called Wells Ferry and later Coryell’s Ferry.

The borough was rechristened after a fire in 1790 destroyed several mills owned by local businessman Benjamin Parry. He rebuilt them as the Newly introduced Hope Mills, inspiring the town’s optimistic new name.

By the late 19th century, New Hope had gained a reputation as an art colony and emerged as a major hub for American and Pennsylvania Impressionists, including William Langson Lathrop, Edward Willis Redfield, and Daniel Garber.

According to recent reports, "Newly introduced Hope definitely has an architectural richness that's been developed over centuries," indicates Reynolds. "Its historic buildings' relationship to the river and surrounding landscape give it a character that cannot be created overnight. And the challenge and opportunity for the architects, for Realtors®, and for developers is to respect that history while designing homes that accommodate the way people live today.".

Fey agrees, maintaining that Fresh Hope's success as a thriving housing market is rooted in its past and the borough's fierce commitment to protecting it.

Sources indicate that "The same little river town 5 miles down the road that did not have a historic district, where all the homes were knocked down, would not have that feel of a classic historic town, and would not have that charm, and it could potentially lose it," he notes. "It's really important to us as architects to preserve that feeling, and that's part of the reason why Fresh Hope is as prized and treasured as it is—it's for its history.".

Even with newly introduced construction, a premium is placed on designing in harmony with the town.

Fey and Reynolds frequently work with clients to select natural building materials such as locally sourced stone, cedar wood, and slate roof tiles. They complement surrounding centuries-old structures rather than clashing with the local aesthetic.

It has been revealed that "Most of my clients are very in love with the feel of the historic New Hope and also would like to see some of the amenities of slightly more glass, slightly higher ceilings," notes the architect. "So when we are doing additions on the traditional homes or existing historic housing stock, our goal is to contribute to the street.".

Despite its modest size, New Hope commands an impressively broad appeal. Esser and Fey say buyers range from locals looking to upgrade or build their dream homes to affluent transplants from neighboring New York, Philadelphia, and New Jersey hunting for a primary residence or weekend pied-à-terre, alongside retirees drawn to Pennsylvania's favorable tax climate.

Some home shoppers, however, come from much farther afield.

Reynolds’ roster of New Hope clients includes buyers from the South of France, Sweden, Canada, and Japan, cementing the town’s status as a market punching well above its weight.

Sources indicate that in August, the Philadelphia Business Journal ranked Fresh Hope as the nation's No. 2 hottest luxury housing market during the second quarter of 2026 among 327 markets analyzed.

"That's an extraordinary distinction for a community of this size," notes Reynolds.

Sources indicate that prices have surged accordingly. Reynolds recounts how townhomes originally priced between $1.4 million and $1.8 million jumped to $2 million–$3.2 million in less than three years.

The latest Realtor.com housing data reveals that in October, the median listing price in Newly introduced Hope topped $2 million, up more than 27% from a year ago.

Meanwhile, the luxury-tier threshold—representing the top 10% of the market—was just over $5 million.

While inventory was up more than 50% year over year last month, Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones notes that supply still remains nearly 60% below pre-pandemic levels.

“Demand comes largely from cash-rich buyers in the surrounding region, including a growing share from Newly introduced Jersey alongside the New York metro, who are insulated from mortgage rates hovering around 7%,” she claims.

As always with real estate, location remains paramount.

"If I have something on the river, it usually sells within a couple days, and that can be something, too, that is not turnkey—we're talking about something that can be slightly a shell inside," indicates Reynolds.

Ultimately, what keeps buyers flocking to Newly introduced Hope from near and far is the sheer architectural variety packed into the pint-sized, picture-perfect historic borough.

"The beautiful thing around here is that there's gorgeous properties everywhere, and the home styles do change between the more modern construction, with the beams and 12-foot ceilings, and old stone construction, but they mesh really well," concludes Esser.

Sources indicate that snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in Upcoming York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#53389. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (959 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople.
  • It has been revealed that I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since.
  • According to recent reports, you didn’t fail the program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

It has been revealed that I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

According to recent reports, you didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

It has been revealed that the reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

In a recent development, nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

In a recent development, we all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Recent findings suggest that now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Industry observers note that somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

Recent findings suggest that what would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

Sources indicate that that work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

Industry observers note that you aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

Nvidia, IBM and Fermilab confirmed new tools for quantum error correction on Nov. 16, and the news comes amid a debate in the crypto industry about "Q-Day," the moment when a quantum computer will be able to break Bitcoin's cryptography. As of Monday, the price of Bitcoin stands at $64,580.

In a recent development, nvidia released a latest decoding algorithm, TCBP-JOBS, on Nov. 16. According to the firm, the algorithm delivers up to 13,000x faster decoding compared with existing leading algorithms, and it cuts the computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to 45 minutes.

Nvidia said that the algorithm helps researchers find designs that use physical qubits more efficiently, "shortening the path to practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.".

Nvidia and IBM also confirmed plans for a modular quantum computing codesign platform with Fermilab. IBM and Nvidia are placing Nvidia DGX B200 systems next to IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, and researchers will use the platform to develop and test error-correction codes.

"Making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems that bring quantum processors and accelerated computing together," remarked Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at Nvidia.

A 2022 study by researchers from the University of Sussex estimated that breaking Bitcoin's encryption within a day would require around 13 million physical qubits.

IBM Quantum Nighthawk, which IBM calls its fastest quantum processor, has 120 qubits. According to Nvidia, errors in quantum processors "limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform.".

According to recent reports, in 2024, Bitcoin developer Hunter Beast proposed BIP-360, a latest output type that would protect coins from quantum attacks. In July 2025, Casa co-founder Jameson Lopp also suggested a plan to phase out legacy signatures and move coins to quantum-resistant addresses.

Early coins mined by Satoshi Nakamoto sit on addresses with public keys that are already visible on the blockchain.

In November 2024, NIST proposed to stop allowing vulnerable public-key algorithms, including elliptic curve cryptography, after 2035.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • BrightAI Inc., a startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, has raised $97 million in funding.
  • Smith Point Capital led the Series A round.
  • Many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visible to an outside observer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:37 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

BrightAI Inc., a startup that helps industrial companies detect malfunctioning equipment, has raised $97 million in funding.

Smith Point Capital led the Series A round. BrightAI said in its Wednesday announcement of the deal that a number of other venture capital firms contributed as well. They were joined by GE Vernova Inc., an energy equipment organization that emerged from the 2024 split-up of General Electric Co.

Many industrial machinery malfunctions affect internal components that aren’t visible to an outside observer. As a result, concerns often go unnoticed until they cause a major disruption. Palo Alto, California-based BrightAI develops hardware and software tools that help customers spot issues earlier.

The first component of the manufacturer’s product portfolio is a collection of sensors called State Stickers. They’re small, rectangular devices with a ruggedized case and a long battery life. Technicians can attach them to industrial equipment to monitor for problems that can’t be detected visually.

Recent findings suggest that the motion of a machine’s internal components produces noise and  vibrations that tend to follow a specific pattern. If an industrial fan’s blades rotate 30 times per minute, it might give off a whooshing sound every two seconds. BrightAI’s State Stickers can detect when a machine diverges from its usual operating pattern.

The sensors wirelessly transmit their measurements to a device called the Stateful AI Hub. It runs artificial intelligence models that analyze the data for signs of hardware failures. According to the company, its models become more accurate as the number of sensors deployed at a site grows.

BrightAI offers software that enables companies to augment the data from its sensors with drone footage. A utility, for  example, could use a BrightAI-powered drone to detect erosion at the top of an electric pole. The manufacturer’s AI models automatically draw a square around damaged components to spare technicians the hassle of manually analyzing footage.

According to recent reports, the company says that its software can also collect maintenance data in other ways. A BrightAI-powered drone can read the meters that are attached to assets such as data center coolant tanks to check their internal pressure. Furthermore, built-in support for infrared cameras enables the software to spot overheating equipment.

The third core component of BrightAI’s product portfolio is an AI wearable. The Stateful Wearable, as it’s called, provides technicians with troubleshooting advice in the field. It also checks whether they follow safety guidelines during inspections and automatically turns maintenance data into reports.

It has been revealed that “Our infrastructure is under more strain than it has ever been, and Physical AI has finally become reliable enough to work in the field,” remarked founder and Chief Executive Alex Hawkinson. “Bringing those two facts together is a once-in-a-generation opportunity.”.

BrightAI claims that its products monitor hundreds of thousands of industrial assets across 50,000 sites. Investor GE Vernova, which is also a customer, plans to expand its use of the company’s technology in connection with this week’s funding round. BrightAI, for its part, will use the capital to grow its international presence.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elite university Harvard maintains significant Bitcoin exposure as it holds over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin ETF, a recent regulatory filing has revealed.

Harvard University remains highly exposed to Bitcoin (BTC) as the elite institution continues to hold over 3 million shares of a Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF).

Recent findings suggest that as per Bitcoin Magazine’s Nov. 16 report, Harvard Management Company, which manages Harvard University’s endowment, held 3,044,612 shares of BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) as of Sept. 30, 2026.

The Form 13F filing by Harvard University with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) highlighted that its investment in the Bitcoin ETF was worth roughly $144.1 million at the end of the third quarter.

In a recent development, notably, Harvard did not change its Bitcoin ETF share count during the third quarter. The university held the same number of shares as reported at the end of June.

Harvard first disclosed its investment in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF during the second quarter of 2025.

As per Harvard's Form 13F filing submitted on Aug. 8, 2025, it held 1,906,000 IBIT shares at the end of the second quarter. The investment was worth roughly $116.7 million as of June 30.

The university subsequently increased its Bitcoin exposure significantly.

For instance, at the end of September 2025, Harvard held 6,813,612 IBIT shares, worth roughly $442.9 million. The Bitcoin ETF was the biggest investment that Harvard publicly reported at the time.

Recent findings suggest that later, however, the university started trimming its Bitcoin exposure. For example, during the fourth quarter of 2025, Harvard reduced its IBIT holdings by about 21.4%. Its total share holdings fell to 5.35 million.

During the first quarter of 2026, Harvard again reduced its Bitcoin exposure by 43.1%. This brought down the number of IBIT shares to roughly 3.04 million.

Since then, the university has maintained this number of shares. Harvard's quarter-end share count has remained unchanged in recent quarters.

Harvard University is not the only top-tier American university that has gained exposure to the biggest cryptocurrency by market capitalization.

In October 2024, Emory University became the first U.S. university endowment to publicly disclose its holdings in a Bitcoin ETF.

It held roughly 2.7 million shares of Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust, worth over $15 million at the time.

Meanwhile, in May 2025, Brown University disclosed its holdings of 105,000 shares of BlackRock's IBIT, worth roughly $4.9 million as of March 31 of that year.

Later, Brown doubled its stake, bringing its holdings to 212,500 shares.

Meanwhile, Dartmouth College has also joined the list of universities with exposure to cryptocurrency ETFs.

In its recent filing, Dartmouth College disclosed that it held 201,531 IBIT shares. The investment was worth roughly $9.5 million as of the end of September 2026.

Can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s new monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Recent findings suggest that lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

Industry observers note that “Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” mentioned Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

Recent findings suggest that the time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Recent findings suggest that debt was a massive part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and mentioned the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on upcoming real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and fresh ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb plans to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the firm mentioned in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment problems, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

It has been revealed that “Travel is aspirational,” Chesky noted. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”.

The announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the company’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first confirmed in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

“Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner stated in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”.

In a recent development, for agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has shared the reason the XRP Ledger (XRPL) used code and cryptography from Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, in its early stages.
  • 16 post on X, Schwartz remarked they primarily chose to do so for security reasons and to prevent backlash from the Bitcoin community when the XRP Ledger was still in its early development.
  • The conversation started when prominent XRPL validator Vet (@Vet_X0) pointed out how some of Satoshi Nakamoto's initial design decisions are still present in the XRP Ledger's structure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has shared the reason the XRP Ledger (XRPL) used code and cryptography from Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, in its early stages.

In his Nov. 16 post on X, Schwartz remarked they primarily chose to do so for security reasons and to prevent backlash from the Bitcoin community when the XRP Ledger was still in its early development.

The conversation started when prominent XRPL validator Vet (@Vet_X0) pointed out how some of Satoshi Nakamoto's initial design decisions are still present in the XRP Ledger's structure.

Vet remarked that the XRP Ledger initially used helper functions from the original Bitcoin software, including timekeeping functions coded by Satoshi Nakamoto himself.

It has been revealed that some of those helper functions were reportedly copied by Jed McCaleb, one of the early developers of the XRP Ledger. The original Bitcoin code even included a comment left by the mysterious creator of Bitcoin.

Afterward, Schwartz shared the reason why XRP Ledger developers opted to use the cryptographic options from Bitcoin instead of creating upcoming ones.

"We did things that way in the very early days because we didn't want to be potentially facing criticism that our choices for those core crypto functions were less secure than Bitcoin's," said Schwartz.

In other words, XRP Ledger developers opted to use Bitcoin's cryptographic options to avoid possible controversial security-related decisions when creating a new cryptocurrency network.

Later on, Vet asked Schwartz if their decision helped gain acceptance among Bitcoin supporters who looked at their protocol in its early stages.

Schwartz mentioned it was hard to say whether it helped or not.

It has been revealed that "It's hard to say. Obviously we never got those criticisms. But it's hard to know if we would have," Schwartz remarked.

Additionally, the Ripple executive pointed out that it was uncertain whether the developers could have come up with better options if they had chosen to make their own cryptographic decisions.

"I'm not sure we would have come up with better ones had we made our own decisions anyway," Schwartz wrote.

It is worth noting that the original Bitcoin code copied in the early stages of the XRP Ledger is no longer present in the network's codebase.

According to Vet, the remaining parts of Satoshi Nakamoto's timekeeping code were deleted in December 2014 by former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis.

There are two crucial cryptographic design decisions from Bitcoin that are still used on the XRP Ledger.

With the law signed by President Vladimir Putin, the Bank of Russia officially rolled out BTC, ETH, and USDT for public trading on domestic exchanges, beginning Nov. 17, 2026.

However, qualified investors are not subject to such asset limits and trading restrictions.

It has been revealed that the development points out that Russia has taken decisive action to deepen the integration of the crypto market with traditional finance. The debut indicates surging retail interest in cryptocurrency amid regulatory evolution.

It signals a strategic shift in how traditional exchanges handle digital assets. Accommodating retail clients signals growing confidence in the crypto market’s maturity. This highlights rising demand for coordinated exposure to crypto assets within Russia’s capital markets.

The announcement introduces upcoming entry gateways that give retail investors organized access to the crypto market, redefining how these assets are traded locally and internationally.

In the past, crypto in Russia operated in a highly restrictive, complex regulatory environment. Now, the regulator is moving toward a balance between investor freedom and financial stability. In July, the central bank opened the door to crypto for companies to facilitate global trade. This month, it introduced fresh legislation that allows retail investors to trade crypto within specified limits.

Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.
  • Sources indicate that existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million).
  • Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Sources indicate that existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Industry observers note that fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

It has been revealed that “Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”.

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

Recent findings suggest that “There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant stated in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”.

Yun and Sturtevant mentioned mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant said. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”.

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”.

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

As a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

It has been revealed that “Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he noted. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”.

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

Industry observers note that “If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun remarked in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”.

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale mentioned existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

“Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she said. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”.

Hale remarked jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

“[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she said. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”.

Yun noted rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

Sources indicate that “One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he said. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the big change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”.

Sources indicate that however, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

It has been revealed that “There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she noted. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on new pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:48 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

A bipartisan group of more than two dozen congressional lawmakers said today they’re forming a newly introduced AI Safety and Innovation Caucus to tackle the growing security risks posed by the advances in sophisticated artificial intelligence models.

Recent findings suggest that the lawmakers cited the July hack of Hugging Face Inc.’s servers by a team of autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI Group PBC, which broke out of an isolated sandbox environment, as an example of these risks. They also pointed to another incident involving the now-public Anthropic PBC, which also reported that its agents escaped their testing environments to access third-party systems.

Sources indicate that these incidents have “underscored the need for Congress to better understand these risks and develop policy solutions,” noted Representative George Whitesides (D-California), a co-chair of the caucus. “As AI capabilities accelerate, so do the potential consequences of catastrophic misuse, loss of control over advanced systems and threats to national security.”.

Recent findings suggest that whitesides (pictured) is co-chairing the caucus alongside Representatives Nathanial Moran (R-TX) and Don Beyer (D-Virginia). In a post on X, they stressed the need for bipartisan collaboration to create the basic policy guardrails for AI safety, citing the growing concerns of the American public.

It has been revealed that does it feel like there's a new tech or AI crisis every day? Recent headlines are raising serious concerns about our digital safety and security.

Today, I'm joining @RepDonBeyer, @RepNateMoran, and over 20 of our colleagues to launch the bipartisan AI Safety and Innovation… pic.twitter.com/bhMyygy1J6.

— Rep. George Whitesides (@Rep_Whitesides) November 19, 2026.

Sources indicate that the 26-member caucus includes seven Republicans, which is a surprising number given that the White House administration under President Donald Trump has strongly opposed any heavy-handed regulation of the AI industry. The goal of the caucus is to identify “targeted solutions” that ensure AI remains under control without derailing innovation and threatening America’s lead in the industry.

Whitesides noted the lawmakers will focus on two things: proposing legislation to augment AI safety, and responding quickly to high-profile security incidents by gathering developers, independent experts and government officials to brief lawmakers and come up with solutions.

Industry observers note that “We want to be a conduit through which effective, responsible legislation can be refined and brought to the floor of the House,” Whitesides told Politico in an interview. He remarked the group will work together to propose, provide feedback and endorse new AI legislation. He believes there’s an urgent need for this, because most other groups within the House are more focused on educating members or creating legislation within their own parties, he said.

Another thing the caucus intends to do is to pursue relationships with outside AI experts who can help lawmakers to navigate complex policy decisions. It also wants to help raise public awareness around AI and its safety challenges, and ensure members outside of relevant committees have the tools they need to contribute to new legislation and debate.

In the recent midterm elections, Americans made it clear that AI is becoming a major concern for governance. Moreover, a recent survey revealed that 43% of Americans don’t trust either of the two major political parties to properly get a grip on AI safety, according to a one-pager that accompanied the press release.

“Artificial intelligence affects every American, and it should not be a partisan glitch,” Moran said. “This caucus gives us a place to find the areas of consensus, set partisanship aside and put smart, targeted policies in place so we can innovate while we keep people safe. Congress needs to be prepared.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • California-born sculptor Chester Beach worked out of a Newly introduced York City studio between 1907 and 1952, nabbing high-profile commissions from the Panama-Pacific International Exposition, as well as the 1928 Summer Olympics.
  • But, like many artists, he carved out space for a pastoral retreat away from the hustle and bustle.
  • It has been revealed that in 1917, after living in Rome for a brief period, he and his wife, Eleanor Beach, established a home in Brewster, NY, in Putnam County, just 55 miles north of the city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

California-born sculptor Chester Beach worked out of a Newly introduced York City studio between 1907 and 1952, nabbing high-profile commissions from the Panama-Pacific International Exposition, as well as the 1928 Summer Olympics.

But, like many artists, he carved out space for a pastoral retreat away from the hustle and bustle.

It has been revealed that in 1917, after living in Rome for a brief period, he and his wife, Eleanor Beach, established a home in Brewster, NY, in Putnam County, just 55 miles north of the city. They named the Arts & Crafts-style estate OldWalls.

Now these 10.49 acres—including four buildings, comprising a compound—is looking for a latest steward.

It has been revealed that "There have only been three owners including the original family that owned it up until 2009," notes listing agent Will Stuart, of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Newly introduced England Properties. "My sellers have been there for two years.".

Listing for $4,150,000, the fresh owner won't be the first to seek a deeper connection to nature while still being close to Manhattan.

Stuart notes that this eight-bedroom, 6.5-bath spread is exceptionally tied to its origins.

In a recent development, "Each owner has become a steward of the property and has preserved extensive family photographs, memoirs and documents, and have really kept the story going, which is rare with these kinds of properties," he indicates. "A lot of times the information gets lost along the way. The story has been preserved so well.".

In a recent development, the estate includes a four-bedroom stone residence with plaster walls, hand-crafted stonework and stained glass. There’s also a separate guest studio with a kitchen, bath, sleeping loft and stone fireplace. And, a two-bedroom guest cottage dating back to the 1940s with cozy amenities such as a fireplace and screened-in porch.

Another way the property has been preserved is through art the original owners brought into the house.

In a recent development, tiles collected from Spain, Guatemala and Italy are laid into the floor, says Stuart. He adds that "there’s actually a cluster of Roman floor tiles under the dining-room table.".

The kitchen’s chandelier was born out of a turntable Beach used for sculpting. Eleanor’s bird paintings (112 in all) are incorporated into the living room’s ceiling.

“There’s three outbuildings in addition to the main residence that all offer incredible living space and charm,” claims Stuart. “Each one of them has a story and a history.”.

For example, in the detached studio, which was built before the home, are many of Beach’s tools and hardware, as well as the original doors.

Industry observers note that A buyer drawn to that history is who Stuart is courting. But it could also be an equestrian, as the property features a five-stall barn with a spacious one-bedroom apartment. Nearby are run-outs, rolling grass turnout paddocks, a riding field with access to trails, and a riding arena in the sand.

“We have a lot of equestrians that have moved into the community,” indicates Stuart. “A lot of the equestrian people travel to Florida in the winter so they’re here half the year, but most people are here year-round.” Two miles down the road is Old Salem Farm, a 120-acre boarding and training facility.

Above all, the buyer will likely be someone who likes to be near Manhattan but also have a countryside retreat, just like Beach once did.

In a recent development, this mirrors a trend Stuart continues to see among buyers. “People looking for more space, more privacy, but want to stay within close proximity to the city,” he says. “This is a real compound here. It’s someone who is hosting family or guests.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, what do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

On this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

In a recent development, he explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel important.

They also get into handling rejection, taking big risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

In a recent development, shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy states many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

For agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

UPDATED 07:16 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Industry observers note that data center backlash is pushing builders to show communities what they get in return, and public-private partnerships are becoming one answer. As the race for sovereign AI heats up, the question is shifting from where intellectual property lives to where compute runs and who profits from it.

Canada offers a sharp test case. A modern data hall employs few people, but its profits can fund the startups and jobs a region needs, according to Sharif Virani (pictured), chief executive officer of SPUR Innovation Center.

“There’s a big misnomer right now in the world that’s kind of landing from previous tech, where people think where your IP is where the wealth creation is going to be,” he noted. “It’s not the case anymore. You have to make sure your inference happens in your country or in your region.”.

Recent findings suggest that virani spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and host Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed sovereign AI, reinvesting data center profits in local entrepreneurs and winning over residents through public-private partnerships. (* Disclosure below.).

In a recent development, SPUR treats its Waterloo, Ontario, site as an innovation campus with an attached data hall rather than a pure data center. The company reinvests about 10 percent of the campus’s data center profits in local entrepreneurs through a venture studio and takes first right of refusal on their office space and compute, Virani explained. Canada’s Dominion List counts more than 500 founders who have left for San Francisco, he noted.

In a recent development, “We have entrepreneurship at an all-time low, productivity at an all-time low [and] GDP in freefall,” he stated. “That’s really the result. We’ve got to reverse that.”.

Industry observers note that one of SPUR’s early investments went to two international students who had full scholarships to the University of Toronto and internships lined up in San Francisco. Instead, they launched a startup called Auditorium AI and hired staff, according to Virani. The model also reaches Main Street, where on-campus hackathons helped a former long-haul trucker build AI software for logistics.

“AI allows these people who know the problem, who have earned the right to solve the problem, to mobilize technology to do it and make the lives of their friends, families and neighbors better,” Virani said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After an important hackathon that demonstrated how AI agents could autonomously perform payments using blockchain, global payments giant Mastercard has spotlighted the XRP Ledger (XRPL).

Sources indicate that 36 hours. 179 hackers. 70 submissions. At the XRP Ledger Hackathon, developers used Mastercard Agent Pay for machines to explore newly introduced possibilities for micropayments and autonomous commerce, including how AI agents can transact within defined spending limits and with verified merchants. See what we learned about the future of agentic commerce: https://t.co/S4NwQxxuRi #AgenticCommerce #DigitalAssets #AI.

It has been revealed that global payments giant Mastercard recently posted on X about the outcome of the XRP Ledger Hackathon. In the post, the payments firm detailed that 179 developers submitted 70 projects during the 36-hour event in Manhattan.

The focus of the competition was how to enable AI-powered agents to autonomously execute transactions and micropayments, engage with verified merchants and so forth, all while operating within budgets set by developers.

The hackathon was held as part of the preparations for Ripple’s annual conference called Swell. Mastercard, Amazon Web Services, QuickNode and Ledger supported the event, which had a prize pool of over $40,000.

Mastercard published an official article in which it mentioned the challenge given to developers. They had to build AI agents that could autonomously make payments to verified merchants without human input.

It has been revealed that also, the agents had to operate within a specified budget. They had to settle payments using Ripple’s USD-backed stablecoin called RLUSD. They had to do this on the XRP Ledger.

One of the purposes of the challenge was to showcase how blockchain infrastructure can enable micropayments. This is especially the case for micropayments smaller than one cent.

In the future, these micropayments could be valuable as AI agents start buying computational resources or requesting data from other AI agents and then making payments themselves for digital services.

Mastercard’s vice president of digital assets, Michael Broderick, stressed that the organization's technology called Agent Pay for Machines could enable such payments.

The project that won the competition is called Wraps. Its creators are Adarsha Mishra and Hrishabh Ayush. Their project dealt with how to secure user privacy in AI-based transactions. Their project demonstrated a method to prove that search logs were not being saved.

One of the most interesting things mentioned in the Mastercard report might be how the XRP Ledger is increasingly being used for payments by machines.

Mastercard mentioned that over 500,000 transactions are being conducted daily on the XRPL by AI agents.

Also, it’s reported that Ripple has recorded over 10 million payments using the x402 internet payment protocol on XRPL. This comes less than three months after the protocol crossed the 1 million payment milestone on the network.

#53370. Breaking: A Massive 8,300-Square-Foot Log Mansion on 22 Acres in Washington Drops Below $3 Million After a Price Cut

Breaking: A Massive 8,300-Square-Foot Log Mansion on 22 Acres in Washington Drops Below $3 Million After a Price Cut

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A sprawling 8,300-square-foot hand-hewn log home on 22 wooded acres in Greenacres, WA has hit the market for under $3 million after a $320,000 price drop.
  • Built with full timber walls throughout and soaring views of the Pacific Northwest skyline, the seven-bedroom estate offers total seclusion just 15 minutes from the highway.
  • Recent findings suggest that “It's huge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A sprawling 8,300-square-foot hand-hewn log home on 22 wooded acres in Greenacres, WA has hit the market for under $3 million after a $320,000 price drop.

Built with full timber walls throughout and soaring views of the Pacific Northwest skyline, the seven-bedroom estate offers total seclusion just 15 minutes from the highway.

Recent findings suggest that “It's huge. It's a 8,300-square-foot log cabin and the architecture on this one is just stunning. It's hand-hewn logs,” says listing agent Denay Hornberger with Realty One Group Eclipse. “It’s a one-of-a-kind property and the owners added a bunch of beautiful features to it.”.

Completed in 2008, the sellers bought the place before it was completed and finished the construction.

“When they first bought it, the builder had spent too much money building it and ended up having to sell it when it was half done. They came in and finished it and added hundreds of thousands of dollars to this property to make it what it is today.” Hornberger explains, adding she lives on an adjacent property. “With the money that's been put into it, [the sellers have] an eye for detail. I mean, everything about this home has been well thought out.”.

Now the owners are listing it for $2.875 million.

In a recent development, “The thing about a property like this is trying to figure out exactly how to price it because there are no comps to really help you decide where the price is right,” she says, adding the initial asking price was a bit high. “I think we're now right in the sweet spot of where we need to be.”.

The home has seven bedrooms and seven bathrooms with real logs visible almost everywhere.

Sources indicate that “There are similar log cabins but they're not fully log cabins the way that [this home] is. Sometimes you have little bits of logs and then you have drywall,” Hornberger says. “Here, the logs are everywhere throughout the house and that is extremely unique to have that. You feel like you are in a log cabin in every almost every single room you're in.”.

The fact the sellers spared no expense is evident immediately.

It has been revealed that “You walk in and your breath is just taken away. It is so beautiful and it's so grand that when you walk in, you just have to take a moment and appreciate it because the windows are huge, the logs are huge,” she notes. “The fireplace is absolutely stunning, and then you look out the window to just woods and skyline. It's just stunning.”.

The home sits on 22-acres of land and while it seems far away from civilization, it isn’t.

In a recent development, “You're actually 15 minutes from the freeway and you're about 20 minutes from the mall,” Hornberger claims. “So even though you feel like you're in the middle of nowhere, you just drive a little bit and you're back in the mix of things. So, you get the best of both worlds.”.

It also epitomizes the feel of the Pacific Northwest.

“We have that woodsy feel. People like to wear their flannel here and we're kind of a laid-back community,” she explains. “So [the house] is taking the best of the Pacific Northwest and having that cabin-in-the-woodsy feel, which is what we're known for.”.

The amount of land makes it perfect for outdoors activities like hiking and hunting, but the house is also luxurious, meaning two types of perfect buyers.

“If you just want to be outside, it’s a perfect home for that,” Hornberger says. “I think the second perfect buyer is somebody who wants a second home... who's in a hustle and bustle all the time but really wants that getaway that they can go to several times a year, have that peace and quiet from the city, get back to nature, and then go back to their regular lives at the end of the day.”.

#53369. The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (769 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (769 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients.
  • Ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place.
  • Industry observers note that wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

Ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in Upcoming York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

Industry observers note that wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

According to recent reports, that shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an notable question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Recent findings suggest that today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

For these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Sources indicate that going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

Recent findings suggest that the mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

When a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

According to recent reports, A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

At The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

Start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

According to recent reports, invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

As brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

Local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.
