📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pulley, a development technology company that helps multifamily and commercial development projects navigate permitting and approvals, has raised $64 million in new funding to expand its AI-driven services, the company unveiled this week.
  • The financing includes a $41 million Series B round led by Jump Capital with participation from Catalyst Investors, and a $23 million Series A round led by CRV and Susa Ventures.
  • Pulley has partnered with multifamily developers like Wood Partners, as well as large retailers, restaurants, banks, and manufacturers, including Amazon, Starbucks, JLL and Meta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pulley, a development technology company that helps multifamily and commercial development projects navigate permitting and approvals, has raised $64 million in new funding to expand its AI-driven services, the company unveiled this week.

The financing includes a $41 million Series B round led by Jump Capital with participation from Catalyst Investors, and a $23 million Series A round led by CRV and Susa Ventures. Pulley noted the capital follows 5x year-over-year growth in annual recurring revenue and will support both expansion of its permitting business and fresh products aimed at compressing pre-construction timelines.

Pulley has partnered with multifamily developers like Wood Partners, as well as large retailers, restaurants, banks, and manufacturers, including Amazon, Starbucks, JLL and Meta.

Pulley operates in entitlement, due diligence and approvals, a part of the development lifecycle that has grown increasingly complex for multifamily and commercial real estate. The firm estimates that 80% of project time is now spent before construction begins, as developers navigate zoning, environmental review, design iterations and building codes that vary widely across jurisdictions.

Industry observers note that “The speed at which we build is one of the most crucial challenges facing America over the next decade,” remarked Charlie Jacobson, Pulley co-founder and CEO, in the announcement. “To remain a global leader in AI, bring manufacturing back home, reach energy independence and sustain job growth, we need to build orders of magnitude faster. The single biggest lever to building faster is to get started faster.”.

Pulley noted it combines AI-powered tools with a nationwide team of more than 75 licensed experts and a proprietary regulatory database to help clients secure approvals “faster and more predictably.” The tech giant reports that it has supported $21 billion in commercial construction projects across all 50 states and thousands of cities and counties, saving customers a combined 11,750 weeks of project time.

Pulley’s services include diligence, approval strategies, construction blueprint reviews and coordination with local agencies. The firm also participates in private plan review programs, allowing it to approve building prepares directly in place of local jurisdictions in more than 2,000 cities and counties, according to the announcement.

The manufacturer remarked customers typically see just one round of comments from permitting authorities per project, and more than 40% of projects are approved without any feedback. Pulley reported that projects on its system have received 65% fewer review comments this year compared with 2025, as its models and rules engine learn from each submission.

With the upcoming funding, Pulley looks to extend beyond permitting into other pre-construction decisions that affect cost and schedule. New capabilities will combine zoning and permitting data with utility availability, local sentiment and other constraints to help owners and developers evaluate sites and programs.

Pulley is also rolling out AI-assisted drawing review designed to flag building code compliance issues earlier in design, reducing redesign cycles and surprises during strategy check.

Industry observers note that lengthy permitting and entitlement timelines are a major driver of project risk and carrying costs for residential and commercial developers, particularly in high-growth markets where local agencies are understaffed and regulations are changing quickly. For build-to-rent sponsors, single-family developers and multifamily owners, a slow or unpredictable approvals process can derail capital plans and delay unit delivery into tight markets.

Recent findings suggest that tools that standardize and partially automate permitting, codify jurisdictional rules and centralize reviewer feedback are increasingly seen as a way to protect returns and reduce soft costs. Pulley’s growth and new capital signal continued investor interest in technology focused on the “paper side” of development rather than just construction itself, and could accelerate adoption of private plan review and AI-enabled compliance checks across more jurisdictions.

#53333. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (835 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that want to price more precisely?
  • When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

According to recent reports, expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

In a recent development, A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Industry observers note that suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

It has been revealed that that’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

Industry observers note that when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Recent findings suggest that maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

According to recent reports, this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

According to recent reports, listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

Industry observers note that twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Industry observers note that find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Industry observers note that sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

In a recent development, roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

Inference pushes AI to smaller sites, making the data layer the deciding factor

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that inference is moving to the center of enterprise AI spending, and the AI data layer is emerging as the piece that decides whether those investments pay off.
  • That shift is putting storage companies with roots in high-performance computing at the center of the AI conversation.
  • “As inference is off the charts in terms of utilization, the data layer is what makes a difference,” Bouzari said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:09 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Recent findings suggest that inference is moving to the center of enterprise AI spending, and the AI data layer is emerging as the piece that decides whether those investments pay off. As GPU costs climb and component shortages persist, the architecture behind AI is shifting from a handful of massive facilities toward a distributed web of smaller sites.

That shift is putting storage companies with roots in high-performance computing at the center of the AI conversation. Turning data into insight at an acceptable cost now depends on a resilient, secure data engine built for GPU efficiency, according to Alex Bouzari (pictured), co-founder and chief executive officer of DataDirect Networks Inc.

“As inference is off the charts in terms of utilization, the data layer is what makes a difference,” Bouzari said. “Costs are skyrocketing. GPUs are becoming more and more powerful, but also more and more expensive.”.

It has been revealed that bouzari spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how inference, cost pressure and shortages are reshaping AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.).

The first wave of AI buildouts concentrated GPUs in large, power-hungry facilities. Inference changes that math because it needs to run close to consumers and their data, Bouzari explained. Communities are also pushing back on giant monolithic data centers, he added.

Sources indicate that “Now, what is happening with inference, you need to supplement that with smaller footprints. Let’s call them data centers, 1 megawatt, 2 megawatt, 5 megawatts. And those need to reside where the action is taking place, where the autonomous driving is happening, where physical AI is happening, where the sensor data is,” Bouzari noted.

Connecting small pods back to large AI factories requires a different approach to data. DDN is building a software layer that spans many types of hardware, a direction reflected in its recent move to free its EXAScaler file system from DDN’s own hardware. The goal is to squeeze more use out of very expensive gear, according to Bouzari.

“It is a software layer that needs to accommodate the different types of hardware because, look, the costs being so high, people want to be able to maximize the utilization over an extended period of time, just like it was in high-performance computing,” Bouzari said.

Recent findings suggest that the scale of spending has changed dramatically. A couple hundred million dollars once funded the world’s fastest supercomputer but now buys 15 to 20 racks of equipment, Bouzari noted. Shortages of GPUs, memory and solid-state drives are colliding with tighter budget scrutiny.

“On the one hand, you have budgetary constraints and the need to extract as much value as you can from your investment,” Bouzari said. “On the other hand, you have the shortages. And so a data layer that can do a lot more with a lot less infrastructure, the smaller footprint is extremely valuable.”.

According to recent reports, that thinking extends into the enterprise. DDN’s Enterprise AI HyperPOD packages CPUs, GPUs, networking and storage into a rack that can drop into existing corporate sites with available power. Keeping the pod on-premises also gives companies tighter control over their data, Bouzari explained.

“I think we’re entering an era where we will see a blossoming of smaller footprint pods being deployed in enterprises globally,” Bouzari remarked.

Sources indicate that bouzari framed the AI data layer as the counterpart to accelerated compute, with Nvidia Corp. supplying the processing and DDN supplying the data. As inference and agents take over, the data side carries more weight, he said: “You need both to make it successful. But the data engine, I think, is becoming increasingly notable as inference and agentic is really becoming the predominant way to utilize AI and get value out of it.”.

Satoshi-Era Bitcoin Holder Wakes Up After 15 Years, Refuting $250 Billion ‘Lost’ Claim

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A Bitcoin address that had not moved coins since February 2011 transferred 75 BTC on Nov.
  • The address is listed as a defendant in a $250 billion lawsuit in Fresh York Supreme Court, in which the plaintiffs are trying to have early Bitcoin wallets declared "lost." Galaxy Research noted that several other addresses from the same list have also moved coins in 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. A Bitcoin address that had not moved coins since February 2011 transferred 75 BTC on Nov. 17, according to Galaxy Research. At the current price of $64,935 per BTC, the coins are worth around $4.87 million.

The address is listed as a defendant in a $250 billion lawsuit in Fresh York Supreme Court, in which the plaintiffs are trying to have early Bitcoin wallets declared "lost." Galaxy Research noted that several other addresses from the same list have also moved coins in 2026.

It has been revealed that according to Galaxy Research analysts, early on Nov. 17, in block 976,209, the address 1ALpEWtXApR19hLXvcG8NfkPyGsUMhFPMS sent coins for the first time. It was first funded on Feb. 8, 2011. At that time, Bitcoin was trading at about $0.90. After 15.8 years, the coins went to an unknown address with a 399-satoshi fee, or about 26 cents, for a paper gain of more than 7,000,000%.

Onchain databases list the wallet as Noah Doe #3409 (Salomon Client Dusted). That label is how it ended up among the defendants in the high-profile case ABC Company, XYZ Company, and Noah Doe v. John Does 1–39,069.

In a recent development, according to the lawsuit, an anonymous plaintiff using the pseudonym Noah Doe and two companies want the rights to 39,069 Bitcoin wallets that have not moved coins for more than five years. The plaintiffs mentioned that these wallets hold about 3.8 million BTC, and at the current price, the coins are worth around $250 billion.

The plaintiffs filed the lawsuit under New York's lost-and-found law, Article 7-B of the Personal Property Law. Under the law, a person who finds lost property has to give it to the police, and the property goes to the finder if the owner does not claim it in time. In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs valued each address at less than $10, and they argued that the waiting period for such items was one year.

Industry observers note that they "found" dormant addresses with an algorithm, saved them onto USB flash drives and took them to the Newly introduced York Police Department (NYPD). Then they served the owners on the blockchain, through microtransactions with embedded messages (OP_RETURN). The practice is known as "dusting," and the campaign is tied to Salomon Brothers Strategic Advisors. Once the waiting period ran out, the plaintiffs asked the court to recognize the coins as theirs.

It has been revealed that the case has been put on hold several times over motions to dismiss and amicus curiae briefs from outside experts. At a hearing on Sept. 8, the Bitcoin Policy Institute asked to intervene as a defendant, and The Digital Chamber asked to join the case as amicus curiae. Galaxy Research described it as a case "in which anonymous plaintiffs are seeking to claim legal title over Satoshi's coins.".

Galaxy Research's Will Owens, who attended the hearing, mentioned that The Digital Chamber's arguments were "well pleaded" and that "the judge sounded sympathetic to them.".

Critics of the lawsuit argue that Article 7-B was written for things you can pick up and hand over for safekeeping. It wasn't written for blockchain records when the "finder" doesn't hold the private keys.

In September, Galaxy head of research Alex Thorn also said that the Lost and Found Property Law includes "protection from 'Noah Doe-style' dormancy attacks on legal ownership.".

#53329. West Capital Lending hit with 1099 independent contractor suit

West Capital Lending hit with 1099 independent contractor suit

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A former branch manager has filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against West Capital Lending (WCL), renewing questions about how mortgage companies use independent contractors and 1099 compensation structures for their staff in California.
  • According to recent reports, in a complaint filed Nov.
  • WCL and Heaps did not respond to HousingWire’s requests for comment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A former branch manager has filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against West Capital Lending (WCL), renewing questions about how mortgage companies use independent contractors and 1099 compensation structures for their staff in California.

According to recent reports, in a complaint filed Nov. 12 in the Superior Court of California for the County of Orange, Jason Heaps alleges that Irvine-based WCL misclassified him and other California workers as independent contractors, depriving them of wages, breaks and other protections owed to employees under state labor law.

WCL and Heaps did not respond to HousingWire’s requests for comment.

Recent findings suggest that according to the complaint, Heaps began working for WCL in November 2023 as a branch manager. In January 2024, he also took on internal technology responsibilities, including customer relationship management (CRM) administration, software development and systems integration. His employment ended in September 2025.

Industry observers note that heaps claims WCL classified him as a 1099 independent contractor while paying him a fixed recurring amount regardless of hours worked and still exercising control over his work. He alleges he reported to a manager, worked from an assigned office in Irvine, did not submit invoices, regularly worked more than 40 hours per week without overtime pay and did not receive his final paycheck after his employment ended.

Industry observers note that “This treatment was not merely occasional, but reflected Defendants’ pattern and practice of willfully misclassifying Defendants’ employees as independent contractors,” the lawsuit states.In a statement to HousingWire, Morgan & Morgan founder John Morgan and attorney Michael Sigall, who represent the plaintiff, stated they had filed “a class action lawsuit against West Capital Lending, Inc. alleging the firm misclassified workers as independent contractors when they should have been treated as employees.”“As a result, workers were allegedly denied basic wage and hour protections California law guarantees. Hardworking people deserve to be paid every dollar they’ve earned, and we are committed to holding West Capital accountable,” they wrote.

Sources indicate that WCL, which has about 1,900 sponsored LOs and originated about $10.8 billion year-to-date, has been the target of several lawsuits over its business and employment practices in recent years. Competitors, including loanDepot and Griffin Funding, along with former employees, have filed actions challenging the firm’s model. WCL has denied wrongdoing in those cases.

The 1099 independent contractor structure is also part of loanDepot’s ongoing lawsuit against WCL. In that case, loanDepot alleged that WCL misclassified about 600 loan officers as independent contractors, paying them on a 1099 basis and avoiding employment-related costs.

“loanDepot’s investigation has revealed that all of its former California loan originators poached by WCL who still hold California licenses to originate loans switched from operating under the standard MLO license issued by the Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI), which requires mortgage loan originators to be employees of their sponsoring lender, to a ‘real estate salesperson with MLO endorsement’ license issued by the DRE [Department of Real Estate] after joining WCL,” the loanDepot complaint states.

Sources indicate that the loanDepot complaint alleges that WCL’s California LOs perform exclusively mortgage loan origination duties, not real estate sales activities. WCL allegedly classifies its California originators as independent contractors while treating those in other states as employees. (WCL also sued loanDepot, alleging Truth in Lending Act violations).

In a recent development, california Labor Code Section 2775 codifies the so-called ABC test for determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor. However, Section 2778(c)(1) excludes qualifying real estate licensees from the ABC test and directs their classification to California Business and Professions Code Section 10032(b).

That provision allows real estate brokers and salespersons to establish their relationship as either employer-employee or independent contractor. For other purposes under the Labor Code, the Borello multifactor test, which is a more flexible, fact-specific analysis, generally applies.Under the ABC test, which applies to most workers, an individual is presumed to be an employee unless the hiring entity establishes all three conditions: The worker is free from the tech giant’s control and direction, both under the contract and in practice; performs work outside the usual course of the company’s business; and is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation or business of the same nature as the work performed.

In the Heaps case, the complaint asserts that WCL’s treatment of the plaintiff “cannot meet any part of the ABC Test and Defendants knew it.”.

The DFPI referred questions about this licensing and employment model to the DRE, which did not respond to requests for comment. The Department of Industrial Relations, which enforces labor law, also did not respond to questions.

The use of 1099 models for loan originators and branch personnel has become a flashpoint in California, where some lenders argue that compliance-focused firms are at a competitive disadvantage.

Alan Pezeshkian, president of California-based House America Financial, said he is not opposed to 1099 compensation structures in principle but is concerned about inconsistent application of labor and tax standards.

Sources indicate that “When companies gain a competitive advantage by circumventing employment and tax laws, it creates an uneven playing field and penalizes those of us who make compliance a priority,” Pezeshkian remarked. “Let’s call it what it is: when a manufacturer improperly classifies employees as independent contractors to avoid payroll taxes and other employment obligations, that’s not innovation, that’s just gaming the system. And when that becomes a recruiting strategy, companies that follow the rules are effectively being punished for doing the right thing.”.

Troy Garris, co-managing partner at Garris Horn LLP, said the inquiry under many laws focuses on control versus independence.

Recent findings suggest that “Under many laws, a worker is an employee if the business can dictate not just what is done, but how, when and where it is done, and by whom. Independent contractors, by contrast, run their own businesses: they set their own methods, use their own tools, take on the risk of profit or loss, and are free to work for other companies,” Garris said. “Some laws make proving contractor status especially difficult, such as under California’s ABC test.”.

Colgate Selden, a founding member of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and a shareholder at Baker Donelson, noted hiring 1099 independent contractors, from a regulatory perspective, is a “dangerous game” because the definition of “employee” touches multiple regimes.

“Regulation Z does not define employees,” Selden said. “If a term is not defined within the regulation, you look to the contract and state law. So, then that’s gray.”Enhancement: This story has been updated to include a statement from the plaintiff’s attorneys.

Ripple-Backed Evernorth Takes Massive $505 Million XRP Hit

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (380 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ripple-backed XRP treasury company Evernorth Holdings has disclosed a significant decrease in the book value of its crypto asset holdings, with total impairment charges amounting to around $505 million before going public on Nasdaq.
  • Industry observers note that per an SEC filing on Nov.
  • This is compared to the firm's initial accounting of the crypto assets at roughly $846.6 million, with an average acquisition or contribution price of $2.44 per XRP.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple-backed XRP treasury company Evernorth Holdings has disclosed a significant decrease in the book value of its crypto asset holdings, with total impairment charges amounting to around $505 million before going public on Nasdaq.

Industry observers note that per an SEC filing on Nov. 13, the 346.3 million XRP tokens that Evernorth Holdings owned had a book value of just $341.9 million as of Sept. 30, 2026.

This is compared to the firm's initial accounting of the crypto assets at roughly $846.6 million, with an average acquisition or contribution price of $2.44 per XRP. This represents a nearly 60% decline in book value.

Industry observers note that as per the latest filing, Evernorth recorded around $271 million in XRP impairment charges in the first nine months of 2026. This is in addition to the $233.7 million in impairment charges recorded in 2025.

Interestingly, only $6.9 million of the recent impairment charges occurred in the third quarter.

This also explains why Evernorth's XRP assets had a book value so far below their market value at the end of September.

Recent findings suggest that evernorth calculates impairments based on the lowest observable intraday price of XRP for each batch of tokens acquired. Once the assets are written down, the company is unable to reverse the previous losses if the price rises.

For reference, on Sept. 30, XRP closed the day trading at around $1.49 on Coinbase. At that price, Evernorth's 346.3 million XRP tokens would have been worth roughly $516 million, much higher than the disclosed book value of $341.9 million.

Industry observers note that the recent disclosure comes around a month after Evernorth completed its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II on Oct. 9. It started trading on Nasdaq under the symbol XRPN on Oct. 12.

Following the business combination, Evernorth held around 473 million XRP tokens and had also raised gross cash proceeds of around $300 million.

Its investors include Ripple, SBI Group, Arrington Capital, Pantera Capital, Kraken and GSR.

On Oct. 14, Evernorth confirmed collaborations with Ripple, Kraken, Coinbase and BitGo to implement institutional investment strategies starting in Q4 2026.

Meanwhile, its latest SEC filing did not include details on the amount of XRP deployed to generate yield or the returns generated from it.

#53326. Industry News: Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (834 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • In a recent development, the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

In a recent development, the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont stated in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

According to recent reports, “The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon remarked in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

Sources indicate that the terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

In a recent development, “Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan mentioned in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an key step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Industry observers note that inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

Industry observers note that “I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s notable to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker remarked workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Recent findings suggest that tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

Industry observers note that “A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker stated. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Housing groups cheer Senate passage of milestone permitting bill

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on Thursday night in a 62-33 vote, advancing legislation designed to streamline federal permitting for a broad range of projects, including housing.
  • Sources indicate that the permitting reform bill aims to cut regulatory delays and lower costs for major development projects in housing, energy infrastructure and transportation.
  • Pro-housing groups strongly support the bill, but many environmental organizations oppose it, arguing that it would roll back necessary environmental protections and promote more fossil fuel consumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the U.S. Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on Thursday night in a 62-33 vote, advancing legislation designed to streamline federal permitting for a broad range of projects, including housing.

Sources indicate that the permitting reform bill aims to cut regulatory delays and lower costs for major development projects in housing, energy infrastructure and transportation. It is likely one of the last bipartisan measures this Congress will vote on before the 120th Congress is sworn in shortly after the newly introduced year.

Pro-housing groups strongly support the bill, but many environmental organizations oppose it, arguing that it would roll back necessary environmental protections and promote more fossil fuel consumption.

Recent findings suggest that BAAJA now heads to the U.S. House of Representatives, which is widely expected to vote on the measure before the fresh Congress is sworn in on January 3. However, the clock is ticking, as the House is already on Thanksgiving recess. That leaves about a month for the House to either pass the Senate’s version or reconcile any differences between the two chambers.

If the bill doesn’t reach President Trump’s desk by January 3, the process would have to start over with the fresh Congress, which would likely change some of its provisions.

Many affordable and multifamily projects that rely on federal funding or assistance face regulatory hurdles that most privately financed housing developments avoid.

Industry observers note that these projects include those backed by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). Examples include housing built using public housing assistance, Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding, USDA housing loans, disaster relief funds and more.

Most notably, these federally backed housing projects must go through National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) reviews that don’t apply to most private- sector development projects.

Recent findings suggest that these reviews, critics argue, add an extra regulatory burden that can increase project timelines by a year or more. Critics further contend that NEPA and NHPA, while well-intentioned laws, are often used by NIMBY groups to delay or kill affordable housing development.

In response to these concerns, BAAJA would streamline NEPA reviews for housing development by:.

These changes would strengthen and expand provisions in the HOME Reform Act of 2025, a bill included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act that exempted small federal housing projects of 15 units or less from NEPA review.

BAAJA would similarly streamline NHPA reviews and narrow which projects trigger a review, allowing redevelopment projects involving older buildings to move forward more quickly.

Industry observers note that additionally, the bill would streamline Clean Water Act reviews, in effect speeding up federal wetlands permitting by shortening review timelines and limiting certain EPA interventions and legal challenges. It would also shorten Endangered Species Act consultation timelines and give states a larger role in federal reviews to reduce permitting delays for residential developments on land with protected species or habitats.

Support for BAAJA spans much of the housing industry. Earlier this month, the National Association of Home Builders, YIMBY Action, Up for Growth Action and dozens of other housing organizations and homebuilder groups signed a letter urging the Senate to move the permitting reform package forward.

On Friday, National Association of REALTORS Executive Vice President and Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn said in a statement she supports the legislation’s goal of streamlining “permitting processes and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens that drive up development costs, delay construction and limit housing supply.”.

“These barriers affect everything from starter homes to multifamily rental housing, making it harder to meet the needs of buyers and renters alike,” McGahn said.

NAHB further argued that BAAJA would reduce land development costs and permitting delays, while also improving multifamily builders’ access to federal housing finance programs. In a statement following the Senate’s vote, NAHB Chairman Bill Owens noted that the bill “will help builders deliver the affordable homes families need.”.

Recent findings suggest that “By cutting the regulatory costs and delays that drive up the price of construction, BAAJA will expand housing supply, lower costs for buyers and renters and increase access to affordable rental housing. With so many families priced out of the market, the House must pass this bill without delay,” Owens noted.

According to recent reports, housing is only a fraction of what BAAJA targets. It mainly aims to streamline the development of a wide range of federally backed projects, including:.

As it does for housing, BAAJA would scale back NEPA and other environmental reviews for these federal projects, while also including other measures to shorten permitting and approval timelines.

In the Senate, 47 Republicans and 15 members of the Senate Democratic caucus voted in favor of the bill.

Senators Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) and Josh Hawley (R-MO) were the only Republican Senators to vote against the legislation, largely because they feared it would undermine states’ rights.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, 31 Democrats voted against it. The legislation has drawn significant opposition from environmental groups concerned that its permitting changes could weaken environmental protections and accelerate fossil fuel emissions.

Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford, for example, argued that the bill “furthers the buildout of fossil fuels, strips away power from communities and Tribes, threatens our clean water and public lands and endangers wildlife.”.

Other critics of BAAJA worry that the bill’s permitting reforms could accelerate the development of more data centers, including on public lands.

Despite the ongoing opposition from environmental groups, BAAJA has bipartisan support in the House. For example, Rep. Scott Peters (D-CA), who backs the bill’s permitting provisions, countered these concerns by noting that it would also fast-track renewable energy development. He reiterated his support for the bill after it passed the Senate.

“BAAJA lowers costs and lowers emissions. It’s that simple. It’s unimaginable that after this month’s election, when the entire country demanded lower costs, we would whiff on the opportunity right in front of us,” Peters stated in a statement.

  • The credit bureau has moved nearly all of its on-premises data centers to the cloud and runs workloads across Amazon Web Services Inc., Google LLC’s Google Cloud and Oracle Corp.’s cloud infrastructure, according to Avinash Singh (pictured), vice president of technology services at Equifax.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:53 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

A multicloud strategy once meant deciding which workloads lived with which provider. Now database providers are moving into the clouds customers already use, and AI projects are raising the value of those migrations well beyond the back office.

Equifax Inc. is a case in point. The credit bureau has moved nearly all of its on-premises data centers to the cloud and runs workloads across Amazon Web Services Inc., Google LLC’s Google Cloud and Oracle Corp.’s cloud infrastructure, according to Avinash Singh (pictured), vice president of technology services at Equifax.

“Their performance optimizer is so advanced that we don’t need to tune a single query,” Singh mentioned. “Just think about that. Fifteen to 20 tickets per day turns into one to two tickets per month.”.

It has been revealed that singh spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how a multicloud strategy is helping Equifax cut billing database tickets. (* Disclosure below.).

Sources indicate that equifax’s global billing system runs on Oracle’s billing and revenue management software, rating and invoicing billions of transactions each month. The database behind it ran on Amazon Relational Database Service for Oracle until it hit a 65-terabyte ceiling. Oracle Autonomous AI Database on AWS, built on Exadata hardware, has room for petabytes of data inside the same cloud, as enterprise adoption accelerates. Because the application stack stayed on AWS, only the database service changed, Singh explained.

Sources indicate that “There is zero code writing because it is just about migrating the data from one database to another,” Singh noted. “We achieved this migration without any downtime.”.

It has been revealed that the results revealed up quickly after the system went live in April. Gathering database statistics on nearly 100 terabytes of data dropped from three to four days to three to four hours. After some configuration tuning, batch jobs that once handled 100 to 200 rows per transaction now process 15,000 to 30,000, according to Singh.

According to recent reports, “Our rating improved almost 200% to 300%,” Singh said. “We are able to close our books way before what we have been closing.”.

According to recent reports, bank of America has disclosed a position in an XRP exchange-traded fund in its latest quarterly 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing, dated Nov. 16, demonstrates that the bank held 13,260 shares of the futures-based Volatility Shares XRP ETF (XRPI), worth about $106,600, at the end of the third quarter.

According to recent reports, bank of America held 13,000 shares of the fund in the first quarter and 13,260 shares in the second quarter, according to its earlier 13F filings. The same filing lists more than $685 million in BlackRock's IBIT, $13.58 million in Bitwise and $950,000 in VanEck.

It has been revealed that seven major banks disclosed XRP fund holdings worth a total of $29.4 million in filings published between Nov. 9 and Nov. 16. Italy's Intesa Sanpaolo disclosed the largest stake among them, at $27.21 million. The bank held 712,319 shares of the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF, worth about $20.52 million, and it also opened a new position of 402,750 shares in the Bitwise XRP ETF, worth about $6.7 million.

UBS and Morgan Stanley disclosed XRP fund holdings of $1.91 million and $116,000, respectively. Most of the UBS position was in the Volatility Shares XRP ETF, and Morgan Stanley held funds from Franklin, REX-Osprey and Bitwise.

JPMorgan Chase held 539 shares of the Bitwise fund, worth about $9,000, and National Bank of Canada held 330 shares of the same fund, worth about $5,500. Bank of Montreal held REX-Osprey and ProShares Ultra XRP shares worth $4,300.

According to recent reports, the crypto portfolio of Goldman Sachs grew to $2.64 billion by the end of September, according to its 13F filing. The bank held about $1.28 billion in Bitcoin ETFs, and BlackRock's IBIT and Fidelity's FBTC accounted for $778 million and $398 million of that amount, respectively. Goldman also held about $1.22 billion in Ether funds, and BlackRock's ETHA accounted for $603 million of that amount.

Goldman held $144 million in XRP ETFs at the end of the third quarter, up from $87 million at the end of the second quarter. The bank's 13F filing for the first quarter showed no XRP or Solana ETF holdings, and Goldman still held no Solana funds at the end of September.

The bank held shares of five spot XRP funds from Franklin Templeton, Bitwise, Canary, Grayscale and 21Shares, and its Franklin Templeton position was worth almost $48 million.

It has been revealed that besides, trading firm Jane Street reported $23.5 million in XRP funds, and Simplex Trading disclosed a $14 million stake in the Grayscale fund. EP Wealth Advisors raised its Volatility Shares XRP ETF holding by 37% to 18,400 shares, worth about $148,000.

A 13F filing only reveals long positions as of Sept. 30. It doesn't show whether the banks hedge those holdings with shorts, or what they did with the shares in October and November. Since then, XRP has fallen below $1, and on Tuesday morning, XRP was trading at $0.966.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1018 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Lock-in effect likely to keep HELOCs, second lien activity up through 2027

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Homeowners have spent the past several years holding onto low-rate first mortgages while looking for ways to access their accumulated home equity.
  • According to recent reports, according to a recent analysis from Benutech that examined county-level mortgage recording data, more than 6 million second mortgages, including home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and closed-end second liens, were recorded between Jan.
  • It has been revealed that annual second-mortgage volume peaked in 2025 at 1.54 million loans, up 21.3% from 2024 and 32.4% from 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Homeowners have spent the past several years holding onto low-rate first mortgages while looking for ways to access their accumulated home equity. As rates have stayed above pandemic-era lows, the lock-in effect has helped sustain demand for home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and second mortgages and is expected to continue into 2027.

According to recent reports, according to a recent analysis from Benutech that examined county-level mortgage recording data, more than 6 million second mortgages, including home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and closed-end second liens, were recorded between Jan. 1, 2022, and Oct. 10, 2026.

It has been revealed that annual second-mortgage volume peaked in 2025 at 1.54 million loans, up 21.3% from 2024 and 32.4% from 2022. Through Oct. 10, 2026, 953,185 loans had been recorded, putting the market on pace for approximately 1.23 million loans for the year, the analysis found.

In October, a report from First American Data & Analytics found that U.S. homeowners held $13.2 trillion in accessible home equity in Q2 2026. Roughly 88% of that equity was tied to mortgages with rates below the market average.

Industry observers note that the Federal Reserve Bank of Fresh York’s Center for Microeconomic Data reported similar findings in its quarterly report on household debt and credit, released at the start of November. HELOC balances increased by $23 billion to $481 billion, marking the largest quarterly increase since 2005. HELOC limits also rose by $31 billion, extending an expansion that began in 2022.

As a result, the news cycle is abuzz with tales of borrowers turning to home equity products. But Anthony Stratis, vice president of lending partnerships at Figure, pointed out that demand has been building for several years, with homeowners using second liens to fund renovations and consolidate debt.

A significant share of Figure borrowers use home equity financing for those purposes, he remarked.

Stratis remarked the demand could outlast the current interest-rate environment as lenders improve their products and borrowers become more accustomed to using home equity to access cash.

Industry observers note that “Home equity has really evolved to the point where it’s a pretty quick way to access cash when you need it for a project or whatever it might be,” Stratis said. “I think that part is going to stay in place, and home equity is likely to have a place in the mortgage ecosystem for a while, independent of rates.”.

Matt Kroon, a home loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage, pointed out the “emotional connection” that borrowers have with their low, COVID-era mortgage rates. But persistently high rates and an aging home stock have led borrowers to inquire about other solutions.

In a recent development, “Since affordability is a major concern right now, people are accessing their equity to make those improvements, or to pay off any higher-interest debt,” Kroon remarked. “Renovations and debt consolidation HELOCs are the main uses right now. However, some other uses include major expenses like a new roof, siding, furnace, etc.”.

Industry observers note that tom Hutchens, president of Angel Oak Mortgage Solutions, agreed with Stratis that his company has seen steady HELOC demand over the past several years. Angel Oak, a non-QM lender, sees most of its demand among self-employed borrowers and those who use bank statement documentation to qualify for both first mortgages and HELOCs.

Sources indicate that hutchens stated borrowers are also using home equity to pay down high-interest credit card balances. Angel Oak’s average combined loan-to-value ratio on HELOCs is in the 60% range, he said.

Industry observers note that “Private capital is getting into the HELOC business. You’re going to start to see more and more HELOC securitizations,” he added.

Kevin Leibowitz, founder of Grayton Mortgage, said that while HELOC inquiries have increased, not all conversations result in second mortgages.

Sources indicate that “[There is] lots of interest in HELOCs, a lot of production in HELOCs,” Leibowitz mentioned. “But a lot of my conversations start with HELOCs, and we kind of pivot into other types of lending because the other types of lending might make sense.”.

The decision often comes down to comparing the cost of a borrower’s existing debt with the rate available on a latest loan, he remarked. While borrowers may be reluctant to refinance a low-rate first mortgage, high-interest credit card balances and other obligations can make a new first mortgage more advantageous.

Benjamin Cohen, managing director and SVP of mortgage lending at Rate, remarked borrowers who might have done a cash-out refinance in the past are now looking at a HELOC or a fixed-rate second mortgage like our HELoan.

Sources indicate that “The math is pretty straightforward. If you owe $500,000 at 3% and need another $75,000, a cash-out refinance puts the entire $575,000 at today’s rate,” Cohen said. “With a second mortgage, you keep the $500,000 at 3% and pay the upcoming rate only on the $75,000. Even if the second mortgage carries a higher rate than the cash-out refinance, your blended rate across both loans can still be meaningfully lower. That can be a good compromise if the payments, fees and repayment terms make sense for you.”.

It has been revealed that leibowitz cited one borrower who had accumulated significant credit card debt after being laid off. By replacing the borrower’s first and second mortgages along with the credit card debt, he noted, he improved the borrower’s monthly cash flow by about $3,500.

Sources indicate that for borrowers with relatively low first-mortgage rates, keeping that loan and adding a HELOC may still be the better option. But HELOCs typically carry variable rates tied to the Wall Street Journal prime rate, exposing borrowers to higher payments if rates rise, Leibowitz noted.

Adam Hopson, chief operating officer of Flyhomes, mentioned home equity can also help homeowners purchase another property before selling their current one. However, the additional borrowing can affect their ability to qualify for a upcoming mortgage.

Recent findings suggest that “A HELOC can unlock a down payment without unlocking a move,” Hopson stated. “Having access to equity and qualifying for the next mortgage are two different things, though.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin (BTC) is facing renewed selling pressure as large holders continue to reduce their exposure, with on-chain data showing that whales have redistributed about $3.4 billion worth of the cryptocurrency over the past two weeks.

According to recent reports, notably, the largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization has fallen nearly 13% over the past week. The decline extends its November losses, bringing its price to a three-month low.

According to analyst Ali Martinez, large entities have sold or redistributed 48,618 BTC, valued at approximately $3.4 billion, over the past two weeks.

“Whales are still reducing their exposure. The selling hasn’t stopped yet,” Martinez tweeted.

The continued distribution suggests that major holders are yet to regain confidence in Bitcoin’s near-term prospects. With thousands of coins changing hands, the market faces the challenge of absorbing this supply without triggering further downward pressure.

Beyond whale activity, Bitcoin’s weekly performance is adding to concerns about the market’s strength.

Analyst Ted Pillows noted that the cryptocurrency has closed six consecutive weeks in the red, a pattern previously seen during bear markets. Trading below both moving averages further weakens its recovery prospects.

“Along with that, Bitcoin failed to hold both the 200W EMA and 200W MA, which is a major sign of weakness. As long as BTC stays below these levels, sellers are in full control,” he wrote.

Meanwhile, several key price levels have given way, leaving Bitcoin vulnerable to another decline.

Mookie, an advocate at Bitget Wallet and ambassador at Dinari Global, highlighted the cryptocurrency’s failure to maintain successive support levels, warning that $57,700 could come into focus if buyers fail to regain control.

In a recent development, “If BTC can’t get back above $66.5K. we could see another drop toward the July low at $57.7K. But if buyers push it back above $66.5K we might finally see a bounce. Still not convinced we’re done dropping,” he noted.

His comments put $66,500 at the center of Bitcoin’s immediate price outlook. Reclaiming that level could help buyers regain some momentum, while another rejection would leave the July low of $57,700 as a potential downside target.

Despite the prevailing bearish sentiment, some market observers believe Bitcoin could be approaching a turning point.

Gordon, founder of Crypto Crib and co-founder of Alphametrics, pointed to a potential inverse head-and-shoulders formation, suggesting that extreme pessimism could set the stage for a reversal.

“All longs have been wiped out, sentiment is max bearish, and retail is going heavy short. This is where reversal happens,” he commented.

An inverse head-and-shoulders pattern is a technical formation often associated with a potential bullish reversal after an extended decline. It typically consists of three troughs, with the middle one forming the lowest point.

Gordon’s assessment offers a contrasting view to the warnings from other analysts. He believes that widespread bearish positioning and the liquidation of leveraged long positions could create conditions for buyers to return.

It has been revealed that however, the formation does not guarantee an immediate recovery. Bitcoin still needs enough buying interest to reverse its recent losses and reclaim key price levels.

At press time, BTC was trading at $59,299, down 5.40% over the past 24 hours.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:58 pm.

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the firm announced Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

According to recent reports, fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

Guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the organization remarked. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the company says other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

Recent findings suggest that “At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon stated in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”.

According to recent reports, breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The firm went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

Sources indicate that fairly, founded in 2023, emerged from stealth in December 2024 with $10.1 million in pre-seed funding. The organization has now raised $32.5 million in total.

Sources indicate that fairly now employs 106 people, up from 25 at its launch in 2024. Co-founder Subechya Person remains chief product officer; co-founder and former CTO Jeff Flitton left the company in February.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz said that the odds of Bitcoin hitting $90,000 by the end of 2026 are slim in light of prevailing macroeconomic headwinds and the growing likelihood that the Federal Reserve may hike interest rates.

During a live event with Anthony Scaramucci at the Digital Assets Forum in Newly introduced York City, Novogratz was asked if Bitcoin could get back to $90,000 by the end of this year.

In a recent development, "Less likely than it was. You need something to happen," Novogratz mentioned.

His gloomy outlook comes as Bitcoin has struggled to rebound after a devastating drop that saw its price dip as low as $62,000 over the weekend. Bitcoin's price stood at around $64,600 on Nov. 17. The largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization has declined for six consecutive weeks.

Industry observers note that A shift in the U.S. monetary policy outlook, namely the prospect of more rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, has been largely to blame for Bitcoin's decline, according to Novogratz.

"At the start of the year, everybody thought the Fed was going to be cutting now," he said.

But high inflation and ongoing supply shocks have forced investors to readjust their expectations.

"Inflation's going up. We've got inflation going up," Novogratz remarked, warning that inflationary pressures could become increasingly entrenched.

"The Fed's going to hike. At least two more, probably three more," he mentioned.

Novogratz predicted that the Fed would raise rates by 25 basis points in December and then hike again at its next meeting.

Recent findings suggest that he mentioned that higher rates, at least in the near term, tend to weigh on Bitcoin. But the higher cost of government borrowing could eventually provide support for the cryptocurrency.

"Yeah, later," he said in response to the suggestion that higher borrowing costs could be a tailwind for Bitcoin.

"First, you're gonna hike rates. Oh, sell gold, right? You're going to go to the dollar. It's so ingrained in peoples' heads," he noted.

"Carry costs going up," he said. Bitcoin doesn't offer the same yield as interest-bearing dollar assets.

"You don't make any interest on Bitcoin in dollars," he remarked.

In particular, Novogratz mentioned that the massive rise in Treasury yields has been particularly detrimental to the crypto market.

Sources indicate that "Literally 40 basis points in like four days of trading. So that's why crypto's down," he noted.

He also mentioned that the massive crypto hack could still be weighing on investors' minds, adding to market jitters.

"I think in the back of their minds is the hack," he mentioned.

Anthropic researcher claims to have proven Riemann hypothesis using Claude

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Levent Alpöge revealed his discovery today on his personal website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:28 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

An Anthropic PBC researcher claims to have used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, which is widely considered to be the most key open question in mathematics.

Levent Alpöge revealed his discovery today on his personal website. Anthropic has not published an official announcement about the news. The firm floated on the Nasdaq a day earlier in a landmark public offering that raised over $93 billion.

Sources indicate that “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a four-page statement. “What I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.”.

It has been revealed that the Riemann hypothesis was proposed in the mid-1800s by its namesake, the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It focuses on a specific mathematical function, the Riemann zeta function, that was discovered more than a century earlier. A function is similar to a software program: It takes a piece of data as input and outputs another piece of data. A function’s input and output can be numbers, other functions and many other mathematical objects.

It has been revealed that the Riemann zeta function’s input and output are both complex numbers. Complex numbers share similarities with regular numbers, but also have many additional properties. When the inputs and outputs of the Riemann zeta function are visualized, they resemble a three-dimensional spiral.

The Riemann hypothesis is concerned with a specific section of that 3D spiral. In that section, the complex numbers outputted by the Riemann zeta function all equal zero. The hypothesis argues that the inputs from which those outputs are derived all include the value ½.

Sources indicate that the hypothesis is considered to be the most important open problem in mathematics for multiple reasons. The first is that although it focuses on a single, not overly complicated mathematical function, its implications extend to a far bigger topic: prime numbers. If the Riemann hypothesis is correct, a seemingly random aspect of prime numbers is in fact regulated by a pattern.

Another factor behind the hypothesis’ importance is that hundreds of theorems operate on the assumption that it’s true. If the Riemann hypothesis is correct, those theorems are correct as well.

It has been revealed that alpöge wrote that Claude proved not only the standard version of the Riemann hypothesis but also the so-called generalized variant. The latter conjecture argues that the Riemann hypothesis holds true for not only the Riemann zeta function but also certain other, similar functions. Alpöge believes that Claude will be capable of proving an even broader version of the hypothesis in the future.

Industry observers note that the researcher detailed that Claude’s proof runs for more than 250,000 pages. He has not yet released the paper. He did, however, publish a version of the proof written in Lean, a programming language used to verify mathematical results. The file contains millions of lines of code.

Proofs implemented in Lean are essentially regular software programs. If a Lean program runs without crashing, the mathematical argument that it describes is correct. That makes it easier for mathematicians to verify newly published proofs.

#53314. Breaking: What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1520 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.
  • Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Industry observers note that ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in Newly introduced York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

Sources indicate that “Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

In a recent development, his co-founder, Jessica Chestler, stated music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be remarked for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

Sources indicate that “I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

Industry observers note that jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

Recent findings suggest that “Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he stated. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

According to recent reports, sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

It has been revealed that natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova remarked. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

Sources indicate that “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova noted. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

According to recent reports, she leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She notes music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

In a recent development, he also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

In a recent development, rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer noted. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea indicates she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

Industry observers note that marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, Upcoming Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

Sources indicate that his Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein stated.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he stated. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

Industry observers note that on setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Sources indicate that bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she stated.

Sources indicate that as for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova mentioned she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

It has been revealed that so the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova remarked, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

Radian Aerospace looks to make its own composite materials for space plane (and for other companies, too)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

💡 Key Takeaways
